description: Event Horizon unites students across Türkiye in AI, engineering, software, research and entrepreneurship. Our members have competed in TEKNOFEST, TÜBİTAK, CERN BL4S and NASA Space Apps, earning local awards. Guided by PhD mentors, we turn bold ideas into real solutions. Join us to collaborate, learn and innovate! We welcome curious, committed teammates skilled in coding, data science, design, physics or storytelling.
summary: FlameBridge is an AI assisted research dashboard that turns NASA's BASS-II campaign, 129 solid fuel burn tests flown in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox, into one instrument for spacecraft fire safety questions. The evidence was spread across 695 files. FlameBridge links every test to its measured conditions, its original source cells and its NASA footage, adds computer vision measurements from 179 ISS video files, and lets users summarize, compare and rank real experiments. This matters because NASA flight data show that Earth's standard upward burning material test is not always conservative in space: in BASS-II a PMMA rod kept spreading at 13.6 % O₂, below its 16 % normal gravity limit. The What If Lab asks which real tests are closest to a cabin or habitat condition and whether that condition is inside the measured evidence at all. For NASA's exploration atmosphere (34 % O₂ at 56.5 kPa) it is not: no BASS-II test started above 22.2 % O₂ and none records a pressure. FlameBridge reports that gap as the next test to run. An AI assistant explains the results and operates the dashboard, but matching, range checks and missing values are decided by deterministic, tested code. FlameBridge never predicts a fire that was not flown.
details:
The problem

Fire behaves differently in microgravity. Without buoyancy there is no rising hot air, so oxygen reaches the flame only by diffusion or by the ventilation flow, and a material that passes a fire test on Earth can behave differently in orbit. NASA has measured this on the International Space Station, but the evidence is hard to use. The BASS-II investigation alone (NASA PSI-25) holds 695 files, about 275 GB: an experimental table, test matrices, a ReadMe, operations documents, 127 PDFs, 265 ZIP archives and 296 MP4 videos. A fire safety engineer cannot quickly ask "which real tests are closest to my conditions, and how far are they?", and a student cannot easily see why a flame in space looks nothing like a candle on Earth.

What the literature shows

NASA screens spacecraft materials with NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, an upward burning test in normal gravity that is treated as the worst case on Earth. BASS-II was flown to test the hypothesis that ventilated materials in microgravity burn as well as, or better than, the same material in normal gravity, and to begin bridging the gap between Test 1 and real flammability in microgravity [1].

In 24 concurrent-flow tests with PMMA rods, BASS-II mapped the lower microgravity flammability boundary as a function of oxygen and flow stretch rate, with a blowoff branch and a quenching branch [2, 4]. A quarter-inch rod spread steadily at 13.6 % O₂ although its normal-gravity blowoff limit was 16 %, a negative oxygen margin of safety of 2.4 % O₂, and the minimum of the flammability boundary lies at very low flows, on the order of diffusive flows [3]. In opposed flow over PMMA rods (0.4 to 8 cm/s, 15 to 21 % O₂), the spread rate in microgravity first rose and then fell as the flow increased, unlike on Earth, and spread was sustained at 17 % O₂ in microgravity against 18 % in normal gravity [5]. Earlier low-speed tunnel tests found normal-gravity limits up to 4 % O₂ above the microgravity limits [6], and a later comparison across BASS-II rods, sheets, slabs and fabric concluded that materials can burn at lower oxygen in microgravity [7].

Future habitats will use more oxygen at lower pressure. NASA recommends 56.5 kPa (8.2 psia) with 34 % O₂ for Moon and Mars missions as a compromise between prebreathe time, hypoxia and flammability [11]. For PMMA, lowering the pressure to 58.6 kPa at 21 % O₂ shortened the piloted ignition time by about 17 %, and raising O₂ to 32 % shortened it by another 10 %, so standard-atmosphere tests underpredict ignition [8]. For a thin non-charring fuel in concurrent flow, lower pressure did not offset the added hazard of elevated oxygen [9]. NASA's Exploration Atmospheres Working Group noted that 30 % O₂ was the highest flammability test level of the ISS and Space Shuttle programs and recommended modifying the standard NASA flammability test to cover the new atmospheres [10]. What follows for FlameBridge: microgravity flammability depends on oxygen and on the ventilation flow [2, 3, 4, 5], so the Lab matches on measured O₂ and airflow plus sample size and geometry, and keeps opposed and concurrent flow visible as a filter. The literature shows the hazard rising with higher O₂ at lower pressure [8, 9, 10], which is where BASS-II has no data, so the most useful answer to a habitat question is often "outside the measured envelope".

What FlameBridge does

FlameBridge connects every BASS-II test record to its experimental context, meaning the ISS run, its measured conditions and its original footage, and makes explicit where the measured evidence ends. It has two modes that read the same data.

Expert mode, for combustion researchers and spacecraft fire-safety engineers:

Home: key numbers of the dataset (129 tests, 6 principal investigators, 123 tests with video) and NASA ISS flame footage streamed from NASA's archive.

Explore: filter all 129 tests by oxygen, airflow, material, geometry, flow direction and investigator, and view them as a table, an O₂ × airflow map or a flame gallery. Data quality flags are visible, never hidden.

Test page: conditions, the verbatim NASA source cells, QA flags and the DOI, plus the NASA video frame by frame with flame overlays (frame, outline, flame only, follow flame), image-derived measurements in sync with the playhead, frame similarity and an illustrative 3D flame view labelled with the geometric assumption behind it. Compare: 2 to 4 tests side by side with synchronized videos and a "what differs" table, including flow direction and image-derived rows.

What-if Lab: the user sets O₂, airflow, material, geometry, sample size and optionally pressure. The Lab ranks the closest real tests, shows how each one differs feature by feature, plots the query on the measured O₂ × airflow map and warns when the query is outside the measured envelope.

Research AI assistant on every page: answers questions in plain language from tool results and drives the dashboard itself (filters, opens tests, compares, seeks video, sets up the Lab). Every AI action is shown and can be undone, including a whole AI turn.

Guided mode, for students, teachers and the public: the Learn Academy, five short missions with quizzes ("What a Flame Needs", "Flames Without Weight", "Two Ways a Flame Goes Out", "Oxygen and the Edge of Burning", "Reading the Smoke"), built on real BASS-II tests and cited sources.

How it works

NASA PSI → Python pipeline → validated JSON → Next.js server → browser, with the AI agent reading the same data through tools.

  1. Data pipeline (Python). The pipeline pulls BASS-II from the public NASA PSI API and builds one JSON record per test. Source cells are kept verbatim next to the parsed value. A cell that cannot be read becomes null with a QA flag and is shown as missing with the reason. Missing is never treated as zero. 40 of the 129 tests carry at least one QA flag (for example ambiguous airflow cells, implausible final O₂ values, a CO sensor over range).
  2. Contracts. Every data shape is a Zod schema. The published JSON is validated against it, with cross-record checks, before the app uses it.
  3. Science module. Matching and pressure checks are plain, documented code, each with its formula, units, citation and tests.
  4. Computer vision (offline). Of the 296 video files, 179 were analysed (133 primary flame videos and 46 still-image sequences). 102 second-view recordings of the glovebox monitors were skipped by design, 10 were not instrument footage and 5 could not be decoded. For each analysed video the pipeline measures flame area, bounding frame and contours by background subtraction (stored at 5 Hz), reads back the telemetry burned into the video overlay (duct airflow, fan voltage, radiometer, clock) with a small neural network, and computes frame similarity (SSIM, colour histograms, flame-mask overlap, optical flow and DINOv2 embeddings). All flame sizes stay in pixels of the 720×480 frame because the footage has no physical scale.
  5. AI assistant (server only). One agent loop works with OpenAI (default) or Claude. It can call 11 read-only tools over the same data the page shows and one UI tool. The server validates every proposed dashboard action against known test and video ids before the browser applies it. The system prompt requires every number to come from a tool result and a plain "not in the data" otherwise. At most 8 tool steps per turn and 10 questions per visitor.
  6. Video. Footage is not re-hosted. The app redirects the browser to a fresh presigned link on NASA's own storage, so users watch the original NASA file. Three short transcoded clips are kept only as a fallback when NASA storage is unreachable.

There is no database and no predictive model. A new PSI investigation needs a new builder that emits the same contract, not a new app. A second builder already turns PSI-20 (ACME Burning Rate Emulator) into 18 daily-summary records in the same contract. It is built but not yet shown in the main views.

How FlameBridge applies the scientific method

Every what-if question in FlameBridge follows the same steps: state the condition, retrieve the measured evidence, measure how far that evidence is from the question, and name the test that would close the gap.

Four kinds of information are kept apart in the data and in the interface: source findings (NASA tables), image measurements (computer vision, labelled image-derived, in pixels), documented calculations, and AI explanations.

Retrieval, not simulation. The Lab is a nearest-neighbour retrieval [12] over real tests. It uses a range-normalized weighted Euclidean distance on measured initial O₂, median airflow and characteristic size (weights 1, 1 and 0.5), and adds one unit to the squared sum for each material or geometry mismatch. A query counts as inside the measured envelope only when a complete test of the same material and geometry lies within 0.25 normalized distance and every input is inside that group's measured range. Film thickness is never compared with rod diameter. The weights are stated as retrieval choices, not fitted physics.

Pressure is treated honestly. BASS-II burned in the glovebox work volume, where nitrogen was added to lower the O₂ (Ops procedure), and neither PSI-25 nor PSI-20 records a pressure per test. FlameBridge never fills in an assumed cabin pressure. A pressure query is reported as outside the envelope on pressure, and the O₂ partial pressure is computed (Dalton's law) only from values the user or the source states.

A concrete result. Set the Lab to NASA's exploration atmosphere, 34 % O₂ at 56.5 kPa (8.2 psia) [11], the kind of higher-oxygen, lower-pressure habitat atmosphere the challenge points to. The Lab reports the query's O₂ partial pressure (19.2 kPa), lists the closest real tests and states that the query is outside the measured envelope: BASS-II covers initial O₂ from 13.6 to 22.2 % and recorded airflow set-points from 0 to 47 cm/s, and no test records a pressure. That missing evidence lies in the region where the literature shows the hazard rising [8, 9, 10], and it is the validation need a new test would have to fill. The PSI-20 summary table lists gas-burner ignitions at 34 % and 40 % O₂ with pressures not identified. FlameBridge keeps those cells verbatim, but they are daily summaries, not individual tests, so the Lab does not match against them.

Validation

Checks that run today:

150 TypeScript tests in 18 files and 27 pipeline tests, run before every merge: data contracts on the published JSON, matching (an exact test ranks first, out-of-envelope queries are reported, missing values are excluded rather than guessed), pressure handling, AI tool semantics, server-side rejection of invalid or hallucinated dashboard actions, and exact undo. A GitHub Actions workflow runs the same checks. Its jobs are currently not started by GitHub because of an account billing issue, so the checks are run locally.

Overlay OCR trained without a single hand label (labels come from the NASA test-matrix dates and clock continuity) and tested on 26 videos it never saw: 99.98 % character accuracy on 16,404 overlay characters (date and clock digits and separators, plus the minus and decimal signs of the telemetry row).

Independent check of the telemetry reading: on 125 primary video files (each file counted once), the duct airflow read from the overlay reached 89.9 % of the airflow set-points listed in the NASA test matrix on average, and every set-point in 104 of them. The sensor responds in about one minute and some recordings end early, so a missed set-point is not always a reading error.

Cross method check of the vision layer: on 85 video files with a flame after the first 5 seconds (each file counted once), the first flame found by segmentation lies a median of 1.6 s from the nearest scene-change boundary found independently by DINOv2 embeddings (within 5 s in 59 of 85).

Stated limits:

  • One investigation is behind the views in depth: BASS-II, mostly PMMA, plus SIBAL fabric, Nomex and a candle, all flown in the same glovebox flow duct.
  • No per-test pressure in the source.
  • The O₂ sensor was out of calibration and corrected by a daily offset, the duct airflow sensor responds in about one minute, and the radiometer is uncalibrated (relative change only).
  • The Lab weights have not been tuned or tested against expert judgement. Flow direction is a filter but not part of the distance. Tests with several airflow steps (67 of 129) are represented by their median set-point, and 7 tests with no readable airflow are left out of matching.
  • Flame segmentation has no hand-labelled ground truth yet. Compact flames read up to about 15 to 20 % large.
  • The records hold no calibrated outcome variables such as spread rate in mm/s. Operator notes ("ext", "blowoff", "no ign") on 23 tests are shown as notes, not as measured outcomes.
  • The AI assistant is limited to 10 questions per visitor IP address on the public deployment, to keep the demo available for everyone. All other features work without it.
  • AI answers have no fixed evaluation set yet. Every cited test links to its record so the user can check.

FlameBridge is not a fire simulator or a certification tool and does not replace physical testing.

How it answers the Flame in Freefall challenge

  • Summarizes: a dataset overview, a summary of each test (fuel, sample shape and size, O₂, airflow, CO and CO₂, sensors and footage) and a "what differs" view for 2 to 4 tests.
  • Ranks: the What-if Lab ranks real tests by documented distance to a user's condition, and the assistant can rank videos by image-derived flame metrics within one investigator's series.
  • Interprets: the AI assistant explains results from tool outputs, and the Learn Academy explains the physics for students.
  • Habitable environments: the Lab tests spacecraft, station and exploration-habitat conditions against the measured evidence, including higher O₂ and lower pressure.
  • Data that supports predictive modeling: a validated, null-aware input layer a modeler can start from, with 129 test records, verbatim source cells and image-derived pixel time series. The test table rebuilds from NASA PSI with one command and the vision layer with a documented pipeline.
  • Next-generation controls and equipment: FlameBridge shows where the measured evidence ends, so researchers can see which test is missing before a finding is used for design.
  • Similarities and differences: tests can be grouped by investigator, material, geometry and flow direction, and compared side by side.
  • Audiences: Expert mode for researchers and engineers, Guided mode for students and the public.

What is new, and what we considered

  • An instrument, not a predictor. With 129 tests from one campaign, FlameBridge does not train a model to forecast fires. It retrieves the closest real tests and states where the measured evidence ends.
  • Data recovered from the footage itself. The telemetry burned into the ISS video (duct airflow, fan voltage, radiometer, clock) is read back by a small neural network trained without a single hand label, using the NASA test matrix and clock continuity as labels.
  • One action system for people and the AI. Every change in the interface is a typed action. The AI uses the same actions, the server checks them against known test and video ids, and every AI step can be undone.
  • Integrity choices: missing is never zero, no assumed pressure is filled in, image sizes stay in pixels and are never converted to millimetres, and NASA footage is streamed from NASA rather than copied.

Use of SI

The Research AI assistant runs on OpenAI gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-luna (default) or Anthropic claude-opus-5-5 (optional), on the server, with read-only tools. Frame similarity uses the pretrained DINOv2 ViT-S/14 model, and overlay text is read by a small CNN trained in this project. The code and documentation were written with AI coding agents (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and Antigravity) under the direction of the human team, which decided the scope, the design direction and every merge. Claude was also used to search the literature for and draft this submission text. The full disclosure is in docs/AI_USAGE.md in the repository.

What we hope to achieve

We want FlameBridge to become a trusted bridge between NASA's archived combustion experiments and the questions of future Moon and Mars missions. The next steps already planned in the project: bring PSI-20 into the main views, add more PSI investigations through the same contract, build a fixed evaluation set for AI answers, and add hand-labelled ground truth for flame segmentation.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: TypeScript, Python.
  • Web app: Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, D3, React Three Fiber and three.js, motion, Zustand, nuqs, Zod.
  • AI: OpenAI Responses API (gpt-6.1-sol, default) and Anthropic Claude (claude-opus-5-5, optional), server side only.
  • Computer vision: OpenCV, NumPy, PyTorch and timm (DINOv2 ViT-S/14), a small CNN trained in this project and run with OpenCV DNN (ONNX), ffmpeg and ffprobe.
  • Quality: Vitest, Python unittest, ESLint, and a GitHub Actions workflow (lint, typecheck, tests, build).
  • Data work: Google Colab and Google Drive for heavy intermediate files.
  • Licence: code and docs MIT. NASA PSI data CC0 1.0.
